items.title: Third spaces perform a star turn in this new Florida master plan
items.description: In a crowded, competitive and bumpy market, residential developers and builders do their best to stand out in a sea of sameness. Some bet that they'll seize a competitive edge by leaning into walkable communities with "third spaces," ones where residents can easily connect with one another and feel a sense of belonging. Wyld Oaks, an upcoming mixed-use community near Orlando, Florida , where construction is now underway, will put that thesis to the test. In October, Hathaway Development became the first developer to begin horizontal construction at Wyld Oaks , where it is building 325 apartment units. That's for starters. Once fully built out, the community is expected to have 6,000 multifamily units and a small adjoining single-family portion with fewer than 100 homes. Residential, mind you, is only part of the plan. Wyld Oaks is designed around a walkable main street anchored by a large park and 300,000 square feet of retail space. Elsewhere in the community, the master plan calls for two hotels, a medical campus, 1.5 million square feet of industrial and distribution space, multiple other parks, an outdoor concert venue and a gas station. For Wyld Oaks master developer Joseph Beninati, the goal is to create a walkable, mixed-use community that functions like a complete neighborhood, with daily needs all within walking or biking distance. “Could you take your car? Of course you can,” Beninati said in an interview with HousingWire TBD . “But the option to walk is going to be there.” With walkability at its core, Wyld Oaks stands apart from the overwhelming majority of new suburban development in the region, which is largely car-centric. Getting the project off the ground has been difficult, however. The original multifamily development, which only just broke ground, was slated to begin in late 2024 or early 2025. The delay resulted from a challenging local multifamily capital environment that has plagued many other Sun Belt markets. We have multifamily, and we're working on retail, food and beverage, coffee stores and grocery stores, all within walking distance,” Beninati said. “Run the list. [Residents] need fitness. They need healthcare. They need a convenience store and daily conveniences, dry cleaning, hair salons and barber shops.” All of the commercial uses designed within easy walking distances in the community will work together to keep residents in the neighborhood, bring in employees to work at the industrial park and various businesses and draw in visitors to enjoy the local shops, restaurants and parks. When everything is in one place, it allows that to happen,” Beninati explained. Beninati envisions a neighborhood where residents can get outdoors and meet one another, whether at local parks, restaurants, the community’s future farmers market or other events. For visitors, he wants a community that is memorable and draws people back in. “For me, some of the softer things would be, are prom pictures getting taken and wedding pictures getting taken there? Or is it a meaningful place that the community rallies around? Is there a Christmas tree, and is there going to be a Halloween event for the kids? Things like that are what make a community something that is memorable,” he said. items.title: RealPlus brings HouseCanary Google Listings to NYC clients
items.description: RealPlus is partnering with My State MLS to make HouseCanary’s Google Listings Program available to its New York City residential brokerage clients, giving brokers and agents a new channel to surface listings directly in Google mobile search results. The integration allows active listings to appear in mobile search with property photos, pricing and agent contact information, according to the company announcement. The placements appear above traditional sponsored real estate ads and include a click-to-contact feature that connects prospective buyers directly with the listing agent. For brokerages, the offering effectively functions as an additional digital listing distribution channel, alongside portals and IDX, but inside Google’s search environment where most buyers begin home searches. In a tight lead-conversion market with rising online advertising costs, direct search visibility and agent-connected lead flows can help firms diversify away from solely portal-driven leads. “We are always looking for ways to expand the value and capabilities we bring to our clients,” Jennifer Boucher, the chief product officer at RealPlus and a HousingWire Insider , said in a statement. “This partnership is a great addition to our offerings, giving brokers and agents another way to put their listings in front of prospective buyers and generate direct connections.” The HouseCanary Google Listings Program will be available to RealPlus clients later in November and will be offered at no cost to participating listing brokers and agents, the company said. RealPlus said the move aligns with its broader strategy of building listing and data infrastructure tailored to New York City residential brokerages at a time when firms are reassessing tech stacks, lead sources and marketing spend. For listing agents, a no-cost path to higher placement in search results could support listing presentations and seller expectations around online exposure. How the Google Listings Program works The Google Listings Program is powered by HouseCanary, which negotiates agreements with multiple listing services to send their brokerage members’ listings to Google. Participating MLSs include Arizona Regional MLS , Bright MLS , California Regional MLS , IRES MLS , Permian Basin Board of Realtors , REcolorado and San Diego MLS . HouseCanary said it also works directly with brokerages, like the three announced Wednesday, to ensure their listings flow into the program via a participating MLS. Brokerages that want their listings included need either to belong to an MLS that is in the program or to encourage their local MLS to opt in. Over the past few weeks, HouseCanary has announced t hat real estate brokerages REMAX Advantage , Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Florida Properties Group , ENRG Realty , Side and The Keyes Company and Illustrated Properties , all RealTrends Verified firms, have signed on to the program, sharing its listings with HouseCanary via My State MLS. These announcements also comes as HouseCanary continues to work through its Chapter 11 restructuring . Under the firm’s proposed plan, which remains subject to court approval, HouseCanary is targeting emergence from bankruptcy before year-end, with full recovery for all approved creditors. Management has positioned initiatives such as the Google Listings Program and the AI platform as core to its go-forward strategy while it continues to serve existing customers. Launched in early 2026 and slated to expand to all eligible U.S. markets this fall, the program is one of several industry experiments that put MLS and brokerage listings in front of consumers in new contexts, potentially changing how buyers first encounter a property and which party — portal, brokerage or platform — captures the initial inquiry. items.title: Education, not operations, are holding back reverse for purchase deals
items.description: Reverse mortgage for purchase loans work much like other types of home purchase financing. Even so, many real estate agents, financial advisers and loan officers don't know how they work, according to experts who spoke this week at the National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA)'s Annual Convention & Expo in San Antonio. Peter Morris, an Arizona -based senior vice president at Revolution Mortgage , said the ideal reverse for purchase prospects are seniors who want to upsize, downsize or relocate. He also frequently works with borrowers who don't qualify for traditional 30-year loans or home equity products due to debt-to-income or credit constraints. Morris said he's seeing rising interest in these financing options among real estate partners. He recently hosted a continuing education course where "I had the most Realtors that I've ever had in a CE class." Senior homeowners with high levels of equity and a need to move are able to utilize the federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgage ( HECM ) program or proprietary programs to purchase their next primary residence. The typical down payment ranges from 45% to 65%, depending on the appraised value, interest rate and age of the borrower. For example, an 80-year-old buyer has a smaller down payment requirement than a 70-year-old buyer since they have a shorter life expectancy. Morris relayed a story about an agent partner in North Carolina with five listings between $400,000 and $800,000. While an all-cash buyer with $400,000 — typically a highly coveted buyer — could afford only some of these listings, a reverse for purchase borrower with the same $400,000 might be able to afford each of them, he told the agent. "You have to educate your Realtor and show them that they are losing out, and they have the potential of making a lot more money with such a simple product," Morris said. "I can show you how you can do less transactions and make more money, because you can buy more of a house in a reverse purchase." Is the process slower? Shain Urwin , national reverse mortgage director for C2 Financial Corp. , and Agi Glukhovskiy, SVP of business support and operations for Rate , explained some of the differences between traditional and reverse for purchase deals. Borrower counseling through an independent third party is required on all HECM for Purchase deals insured by the Federal Housing Administration and for most proprietary reverse mortgages. Reverse transactions also have unique forms, including a Good Faith Estimate (GFE) and a HUD-1 form, rather than the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure forms commonly associated with forward mortgages. Glukhovskiy said the absence of conventional forward lending documents are actually an advantage for reverse deals since they won't have a mandatory federal waiting period. Urwin noted that a handful of states, such as California and Idaho, have implemented their own waiting periods. Beyond that, however, the steps are largely the same as any traditional deal as the process moves from application to underwriting, appraisal , title and approval. The panelists sought to dispel ideas that reverse purchases are slow to close. Glukhovskiy said her team has wrapped them up in seven to 10 days, and although the average is 20 to 25 days, the idea that the process takes 45 days is "absolutely nonsense," she added. Neil Sweren, a Baltimore -based reverse division manager for Atlantic Coast Mortgage , recalled a recent deal that closed in seven calendar days. Angel Booth, national sales manager for title and settlement services provider Premier Reverse Closings , clarified to HousingWire 's Reverse Mortgage Daily that the typical 10- to 15-day process cited by lenders is "absolutely attainable" once the loan is clear to close. Glukovskiy said the keys to a quick closing are finishing counseling prior to the start of the home search process, collecting income documentation, and setting expectations with agents and lending operations staff. Loan officers should read the purchase contract and know every contingency date, Urwin said, as trouble begins when they overpromise. And Sweren pointed to timing: If a closing date gets pushed back and falls within six months of the borrower's birthday, the amount of cash needed to close can change. Simultaneous closings, where the borrower sells one home and buys another, can be difficult but not impossible to pull off. Glukovskiy recommended that sale proceeds should go straight to the title company handling the property being purchased, rather than going to the borrower. Urwin told a cautionary tale about a borrower who took their sale proceeds and paid down a home equity line of credit on another property, leaving them ineligible to use the borrowed funds to buy their new house. "I learned from that very painfully, but those kinds of nuances matter when tracking those funds," he said. Winning over agents and advisers For loan officers who are new to reverse for purchase deals, panelists urged them to study up before they present the benefits to agents. Continuing education courses are a prime way to teach agents, with Sweren saying they often come to his classes to help their own parents or grandparents. Many agents happen to be senior homeowners and may need assistance for themselves. Being the go-to loan officer when a listing includes a reverse mortgage should be part of everyone's market strategy. The panelists admitted that financial advisers may be a harder sell. Urwin noted that because these referral partners focus on cash and assets under management, they may not recommend a client put their cash into a home. But he relayed a success story where an adviser partner took out a reverse mortgage on his own home, then began sending referrals to Urwin when he had older clients who wanted to pay cash for a house. items.title: A Veterans Day reflection for building leaders and the work ahead
items.description: Today, amid the quickened pulse of our nation's political and cultural divisions, Veterans Day gives Americans a chance to take stock of something that transcends the moment's disputes and divides. We have inherited something incalculably, extraordinarily valuable. Generations of men and women who served in the United States Armed Forces have helped preserve and protect a nation where we can live, work, worship, disagree, build businesses, raise families and decide what kind of future we want for ourselves and for those who come after us. Those freedoms don’t exist in a vacuum. They’re neither inevitable nor self-sustaining, though we may act as if we take them for granted. They exist only because people before us accepted duties, endured pain, and made sacrifices for beneficiaries they didn’t know and ultimately never would. Our children. Our children's children. Their children. And on and on. That generational commitment deserves more than our gratitude, though gratitude is where we begin today. And where we need to begin each day. A salute and a deeply felt debt of gratitude are an open invitation. It asks each of us to examine what we do with our hard-won inheritance. It asks us all what we are willing to do to preserve and improve it for generations beyond our own. For those of us whose livelihoods center on making homes and neighborhoods for people to live in, that searching examination resonates. We work in a business community whose homes, neighborhoods, infrastructure and institutions endure. They’re a bedrock for generations. They profoundly nurture and shape the possibilities, the very dreams, available to American families and households. Military service and homebuilding are not equivalent sacrifices. Still, much to learn from the commitment to mission, dependence on others, the discipline of preparation, and the willingness to serve a purpose larger than oneself that distinguishes the best traditions of military service. When gratitude becomes action This Veterans Day, we have a moving example of what happens when gratitude becomes a commitment to act. In Austin, Texas, this week, Lennar and nonprofit Operation Finally Home , joined by country music artist and U.S. Army Reserve soldier Craig Morgan, surprised two military veterans and their families with the promise of new, mortgage-free homes. Marine Corps Sgt. Kevin Gallmeier served a decade in uniform, including combat deployments to Iraq, before retiring medically after sustaining service-related injuries. Army Spc. Jordan Taylor served in Baghdad and later continued serving his community as a firefighter and EMT until a serious injury forced him to retire. For Taylor, his wife Aylynn, and their four children, financial hardship meant selling their family home and moving in with relatives. The promise of a new home offers a chance to regain stability and independence. For Gallmeier and his family, a groundbreaking this week at Lennar's Freedom Crossing community in Killeen, Texas, marked the start of a new chapter. Operation Finally Home founder Dan Wallrath describes the organization's mission as fighting with hammers, nails, and humility to restore dignity and peace of mind. Nothing magical makes these homes a reality. Land must be secured, capital committed, plans developed, materials and products donated and skilled people coordinated through hundreds of decisions and handoffs before families receive their keys. What makes the effort extraordinary is that people across organizations commit their capabilities and resources to a shared purpose, with the needs of two families at its core. That is gratitude expressed through action. And as HousingWire TBD reporter Tyler Williams chronicles in his Veterans Day reporting, this spirit of service spans the nation's homebuilding community, from West to East and from South to North. From PulteGroup and Meritage Homes donating mortgage-free homes to regional builders offering military families financial assistance, and industry partners helping veterans transition into civilian careers, the commitment takes many forms. Behind these named initiatives are countless unheralded builders, tradespeople, suppliers, employees, and volunteers who contribute their skills, resources, and time in communities across America. Their efforts reflect a deeply rooted conviction that building homes and communities also means honoring those whose sacrifices have made our freedom to do so possible. Beyond magical thinking Human beings have an extraordinary capacity to imagine a better future. That capacity is among our greatest strengths, enabling us to conceive of possibilities that do not yet exist and to organize our efforts to make them real. We also tend toward magical thinking : believing that our wishes, convictions, or the triumph of our preferred outcomes will somehow deliver the future we envision without the difficult work required to bring it about. Housing affordability offers a case in point. For years, builders, developers, investors, policymakers, and families have wrestled with the interrelated constraints of lots, labor, lending, local approvals, and lumber — shorthand for the broader building-products supply chain. These five L's often pull against one another. Improvement in one area does not necessarily lead to meaningful progress overall. In reality, getting one right often comes at the expense of one or more of the others. And then there’s the sixth L: leadership. No single technological breakthrough, policy initiative, favorable interest-rate cycle, or election result will solve the interconnected problems of producing homes more Americans can afford. There is no abracadabra. Only the sustained work of learning, adapting, cooperating, and improving remains. items.title: Homebuilders and their partners team up to salute our veterans
items.description: Each Veterans Day, millions of Americans take a moment to honor the sacrifices that our military veterans have made for generations. On a personal note, today I’m remembering both of my late grandfathers. One served in the Navy, while the other received a Purple Heart and numerous other medals for his bravery and service during the Vietnam War. Across the country, homebuilders are marking Veterans Day with a range of initiatives, including special promotions and discounts for military families, mortgage-free home donations and workforce development programs designed to support veterans transitioning into civilian careers. Homebuilders gift homes and workforce development The following are some of the ways homebuilders are recognizing and supporting veterans this year. PulteGroup , in partnership with Operation Homefront, announced that it gifted multiple newly constructed homes to military service members in cities like Anna, Texas, Wixom, Michigan and Richmond Hills, Georgia. Meritage Homes , also in partnership with national military nonprofit Operation Homefront , will donate a brand-new, mortgage-free home to a military family in Gulfport, Mississippi. The lucky recipient of Meritage Homes’ giveaway was Navy Personnel Specialist 2nd Class Maggie Coleman, who served 13 years in the Navy. Coleman will receive a 2,000-square-foot home with four bedrooms and three bathrooms. “I want to give my children everything I didn’t have. I want this home to be a place where my kids and I can share stories and make memories,” Coleman said in a press release. Lennar partnered with national nonprofit Operation Finally Home and country music artist and U.S. Army Reserve soldier Craig Morgan to surprise two military families with brand-new, mortgage-free homes in celebration of Veterans Day. The surprises unfolded Monday evening in Austin, Texas, during a reception in which the veterans believed they were simply attending as honored guests of the foundation. And earlier this week, Invitation Homes announced that it has teamed up with Home Builders Institute to fund hands-on training, industry credentials and job placement for transitioning service members and veterans. Taylor Homes , which builds in Kentucky, Indiana and Ohio, announced that it doubled its "We Salute You" bonus to $2,000 throughout November, giving military members a price reduction on a new home. Tennessee-based Pratt Home Builders , meanwhile, is offering veterans, active-duty military and reservists $3,000 in savings toward a new home during November and December. Buyers can apply the savings toward the purchase price, design upgrades or appliances. Other builders are offering similar incentives in select markets, either temporarily or on an ongoing basis. D.R. Horton , for example, is offering up to $2,500 toward closing costs through its Home of the Brave program in select San Antonio-area communities. Landmark Homes offers active-duty military members and veterans a $1,000 incentive that can be combined with other promotions in Northern Colorado. In Idaho, Hubble Homes offers a $2,500 Homes for Heroes discount, as does Drees Homes in markets like Jacksonville and San Antonio. David Weekley Homes , meanwhile, provides military personnel with $1,000 in Flex Dollars in the Charleston, South Carolina market. Many of these programs extend beyond veterans and military personnel to include teachers, police officers, firefighters and other first responders, grouping them under broader Hometown Heroes or similar initiatives. items.title: Winning in a buyer’s market
items.description: As we head into the end of the year, we are at a truly magical moment for buyers across much of America. Buyers have more houses to choose from, along with the ability to inspect the property, negotiate repairs and make homeownership more affordable . It is something buyers have been wanting for years, but where are all the buyers? Pending sales were recently recorded as the lowest since they started tracking pending sales! Currently, many buyers are holding back for three main reasons. As a mortgage lender or real estate agent, knowing these reasons and how to solve them is the key to helping your buyers win right now. Would I recommend waiting for lower rates? Absolutely not; the lower the rates, the more competition, and it is the lack of competition where true opportunity lies. Reason 1: Rates are high Ask the seller to pay to buy down the mortgage rate . I like a permanent buydown as it gives certainty for the long run. Many buyers can afford the house when the rate starts at 6%, so use a seller buydown to get there. Reason 2: The price is too high Offer less. Many buyers do not know that you can offer less. They are waiting for the seller to drop the price when, in reality, they should just write an offer now with what they want to pay. It is up to the seller to say yes or no. Whether the seller agrees depends on their financial situation and their motivation to sell. I have chatted with clients who want the house, but not at the current price and are afraid to offer $10,000 less. To me, that's a missed opportunity. The seller could be sitting on the other side praying they get an offer. Write the offer. Reason 3: I don’t have enough saved for closing costs Did you know many buyers don't realize they can ask the seller to pay for closing costs? Over 42% of recent sales have seller concessions, but many buyers still do not know you can ask for this. You could have a buyer you talked to last year who was in a seller's market, who is saving away, who does not even know that their market is now a buyer's market. This is your opportunity as a real estate professional to help them get home. Ask the seller to pay their closing costs and help them get home for the Holidays. As I type this, we have buyers across the country negotiating for lower sales prices, closing costs and rate buydown covered by the seller. Does every seller say yes? No, but that is the beauty of the buyer's market; there are so many sellers to choose from. There is tremendous opportunity in the market right now for buyers to win. Help them seize it. Jennifer Beeston is the EVP of National Sales at Chairman’s Circle (NMLS ID: 247743). This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. items.title: Rapidly Growing Electronics Reseller Plots 300 More Franchises
items.description: Electronics reseller PayMore, which opened its 150th store this month, has 300 more locations in the pipeline. Google Maps A PayMore location in Phoenix The Long Island, New York-based retailer has nearly tripled its footprint over the past two years, growing from 58 North American locations at the end of 2024 to 150 as of Nov. 2, with the addition of a Baton Rouge, Louisiana, location. It expects to open around 15 more locations this year, PayMore announced Tuesday. PayMore said it sold an additional 300 franchise locations but didn’t say how many, if any, have found real estate. The company was founded in 2011 and began franchising in 2020. It buys devices including smartphones, laptops, tablets, gaming systems, computer components, smartwatches and cameras, and evaluates the products for resale or recycling. The products it resells “undergo testing and appropriate data-handling procedures,” it said. items.description: While the midterm election results sent a clear message that voters have concerns about the rapid data center build-out, it appears the industry's construction pipeline is still on track — at least for next year. Unsplash/İsmail Enes Ayhan New research from J.P. Morgan Asset Management and comments from CoreWeave leadership in the wake of its unexpectedly strong third-quarter earnings report point to a positive outlook for development in 2027, even if the sector is ultimately expected to lose steam in 2028. “We do not anticipate any impact from the seismic regulatory shift that’s occurred,” CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said during the firm’s Tuesday afternoon earnings call. “We are very comfortable with our pipeline. ... We believe that what has occurred is a statement around how you build. We want to build responsibly.” “So we think that is an opportunity for us to continue to scale our business within the new political reality that exists,” he added. The AI firm's stock had plunged last week after anti-data center candidates swept the midterms, but it has been rallying since then, including a more than 26% jump since the earnings report was released Tuesday. CoreWeave reported $3.66B in quarterly revenue, up 168% year-over-year and beating industry estimates of $3.56B. It has also raised its full-year revenue guidance. The bullish outlook aligns with a projection from J.P. Morgan, which expects artificial intelligence -related capital expenditures to reach $1.5T in 2027 and level off in the following year due to political pushback, Semafor reported . J.P. Morgan researchers said in the report that the legislative pushback to data center construction has “more bark than bite.” Of the 16 statewide moratoriums that have been proposed, just one in New York has become law. The report also found that weeding out speculative projects could be good for the industry. It said of the 430 gigawatts worth of proposed data center projects, just 59% are in active development. “Projects already under construction are generally less vulnerable to new restrictions,” J.P. Morgan Global Market Strategist Stephanie Aliaga wrote. “Future developments face greater uncertainty around permitting, power availability and financing, with delays and higher costs potentially pressuring returns.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: CoreWeave , JPMorgan , Michael Intrator , Stephanie Aliaga

items.title: Royal London Gets Alternative With £105M Of Deals
items.description: Pexels/Towfiqu barbhuiya Royal London Asset Management has completed four long-income property transactions worth approximately £105M, expanding its private markets business less than a year after launching its commercial real estate finance team. The deals span key-worker housing, education and student accommodation, with the investment manager targeting secured, long-term income streams backed by property and its operators. The largest element includes funding NHS -backed accommodation for 215 hospital staff, alongside investment in a London academy school educating 750 pupils and 740 student beds at a Russell Group university. The transactions are part of RLAM ’s push into long-income real estate, using structures including sale-leasebacks, income strips, loans and ground rents, the company said. The investments are designed to provide institutional investors, including pension funds, with predictable and potentially inflation-linked income, RLAM added in an update. “These transactions show how quickly we are turning our private markets ambitions into investments,” RLAM Head of Commercial Real Estate Finance Peter Manners-Smith said in a statement. “There is a clear opportunity to connect institutional capital with real estate financing needs across the public sector and beyond. For clients, the focus is on securing income streams that match their liabilities and meet the needs of UK pensioners,” he added. RLAM Head of Long-Dated Origination Shailendra Shah said the deals demonstrated the range of financing opportunities available through partnerships with property owners and operators. The move is part of a broader expansion of RLAM's private markets capabilities, and the manager, part of mutual insurer Royal London, oversees £212B in assets across its investment business as of June 2026. Its established property operation had £9.1B under management at the end of June 2025, investing across commercial property and alternative sectors including residential, healthcare and life sciences. RLAM has been building out its private assets platform through new lending strategies and acquisitions. It launched an asset-backed finance fund in October 2025 focused primarily on senior secured lending and acquired infrastructure investment manager Dalmore Capital, which brought approximately £6B of assets. items.title: Blackstone Targets $3B Fundraise For Real Estate Secondaries
items.description: Blackstone is raising cash to pick up stakes in real estate from antsy private-market investors. Bisnow/Sasha Jones Blackstone Strategic Partners, the firm’s secondary business, is expected to raise at least $3B as part of the latest fundraising effort, which will be used to target acquisitions of core real estate interests at discounts to net asset value, anonymous sources told Bloomberg . The capital will be primarily deployed into funds with data center, rental housing and industrial assets, the sources said, requesting not to be named because the fundraising drive isn’t public. Blackstone declined to comment to Bloomberg and didn’t respond to Bisnow ’s request for comment Wednesday morning. Strategic Partners' last fundraising round closed in November 2023 with $2.6B in commitments. The latest fundraising effort comes amid growing demand for real estate secondaries as a growing number of limited partners in real estate investments look to cash out early. Real estate secondaries had a record year in 2025 with $20.3B in total volume, with 72% of market volume coming from general partners, the fund managers that run the investments and typically decide to sell, according to a February report from Ares Management Corp. There’s a growing demand for cash now among both money managers and limited partners, the investors that provide capital but take a more passive role in operations, that is fueling Blackstone’s latest fundraising effort, executives who spoke with Bloomberg said. Blackstone itself has in recent months turned to the secondary market to help meet investor redemption requests. The investment giant in September reached out to potential buyers from Blackstone Property Partners to cut a deal that would let some existing investors liquidate. Blackstone Property Partners is a multifund vehicle with $58B in combined assets that invests institutional capital in long-term, income-producing assets, including data centers, industrial assets and office buildings. The secondaries market has expanded at a rapid clip since 2022, when the Federal Reserve raised interest rates and sapped velocity from capital markets. By 2025, general partner-led secondaries had become the fastest-growing segment of the market. UK-based Partners Group launched its own fundraising round for a secondaries program this year, announcing $650M in commitments in June for a fund targeting $1.5B in total. items.title: Rising appraisal defects signals likely stress for lenders
items.description: Rising appraisal defects signals likely stress for lenders By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published November 10, 2026, 5:52 p.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: The reason a recent drop in critical mortgage defects is actually cause for concern. Expert Quote: "Given this quarter's findings, however, appraisal will certainly be an area to watch next quarter" — Nick Volpe, Executive Vice President, Aces Quality Management Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Even as mortgage file defect rates improved on a quarter-to-quarter basis, the increase in appraisal-related problems is the canary in the coal mine for stress in a difficult housing market, Aces Quality Management warned. Processing Content The critical defect rate fell to 1.64% from 1.71% in the first quarter . But this is higher than the 1.51% for the second quarter last year , as the rate would eventually reach 1.79% in the following three months. While defects related to borrower income and employment returned to the most cited problem, increasing to 23.18% in the second quarter report, appraisal-related problems rose by 38.5% to a 4.64% share, the highest since the second quarter of 2025. Since Jan. 28, the mortgage industry has been in what was called the broad production period, as lenders could submit appraisals using either the UAD 2.6 or UAD 3.6 format to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. During this time, originators and appraisers were to use the opportunity to incorporate the new format into their workflows. Absent a waiver, mandatory use of UAD 3.6 started on Nov. 2. When asked if the switchover could be responsible for the rise in appraisal defects, at this point Aces has not seen any evidence in its data that the preparations for the change affected the category during the second quarter, Nick Volpe, executive vice president, said in response to an inquiry. "Approximately 60% of the exceptions were issues on the Form 1033 (post-closing appraisal review form)," Volpe explained. "These issues included: subject property eligibility, description of the subject property, Collateral Underwriter messaging, completion/inspection, and appraisal conditions that were unacceptable to Fannie Mae. None of those would lead us to believe that UAD 3.6 impacted the findings." Right now, it is hard for Volpe to comment on any future impact the switch could have on file quality. "Given this quarter's findings, however, appraisal will certainly be an area to watch next quarter, and it will be interesting to see if and how any of those manifest," he said. There isn't a defect category specifically for UAD 3.6, so any observations would be speculative." In the press release, Volpe pointed out that if appraisal defects hold in the 4% to 5% range in the third quarter data (since these are post-closing file reviews, the loans were originated in previous periods), "we'll want to dig into what's driving it." Refinances are another potential hot spot, precisely because the volume declined. The file which did come through and were reviewed "still carried a disproportionate share of defects," he said. "With rates higher in the third quarter, refinance volume may keep falling, and that's exactly when lenders need to stay disciplined on the files that do come through." Aces noted borrower and mortgage eligibility file issues rose a whopping 60.4% versus the first quarter to an 11.92% share overall, rising to third place. Meanwhile legal/regulatory/compliance defects fell by 17% to 21.52%. Aces categorizes mortgage file defects using the Fannie Mae taxonomy. Other categories with significant findings include assets, at 11.59%, an increase of 11.3% from the prior quarter. But Aces found fewer liability-related defects, at 9.72% and credit at 4.97%. Title company earnings going forward could be affected by the expansion of a secondary market pilot program to reduce the cost of this coverage to consumers. But the early comments from industry executives showed little concern. Processing Content The current iteration is limited to certain loan types, regions and lenders and thus has not had a big impact on title company business. But the recent executive order from Pres. Trump issued on Oct. 22 put an expansion of this title waiver pilot on the table. Now, Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte on Friday afternoon posted on X that he was actively working on expanding the title insurance pilot, with updates to come in December. During Fidelity National Financial's earnings call on Nov. 6, which was prior to the Pulte post, Mike Nolan, CEO said in response to an analyst's question, "it was too early to tell because really all the executive order did was direct the director to think about things. So what comes out of that, we just don't know yet." Later in the call, Nolan cited a National Mortgage News article, which said the government-sponsored enterprises had handled 22,000 waiver transactions to date, which he said was over a two-year period. He pointed out over 3 million residential refinances took place during this time frame. "I would also just say anecdotally, I still do not have anyone in our world here at the FNF family of companies really telling me they're losing orders to the waiver program," Nolan said. On its call, Stewart Information Services CEO Fred Eppinger called the waiver program "old news." The call took place prior to the executive order announcement, although the questioner noted rumors of a potential expansion. "We are not really big in the refi market and I don't think there's many that want to be big in the refi market given the volatility of that business and the low margins that are in it," Eppinger said. On the calls, the continued elevated mortgage rate environment was a common theme, but for some, commercial business was an offset. All four of the large underwriters also noted their investments in artificial intelligence technology to re-engineer processes. This compared with $288 million in the second quarter and $358 million one year ago. "Over the course of the year, purchase orders opened have held up well through August with each month comparing favorably to the prior year before falling behind by 2% for the month of September," Nolan said. "Importantly, we continue to steadily outperform relative to our peers." On the residential side, daily purchased orders opened were up 3% year-over-year, while daily refinance orders fell 11%. But commercial orders opened, which commands higher fees, increased 2%. Total opened orders ended the quarter at 368,000, versus 391,000 three months prior and 370,000 one year before. Data centers, a hot button topic , have been a part of FNF's insured portfolio for four years, with several older transactions already refinancing. "Similar to energy, data centers tend to be higher premium transactions, although comprising a small portion of the overall order count," Nolan said. items.title: Christmas Lights Are Squeezing Homeowner Budgets More Than Ever, but There’s a Way To Pay Less and Still Be Festive
items.description: Christmas lights can bring holiday cheer to your home and neighborhood, but they don’t come cheap. The U.S. Energy Information Administration projects the national average residential electricity price at about 18 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2026—roughly 37% higher than in 2020. This translates to the highest utility bills some homeowners have ever seen, made worse during times of the year when more electricity is needed. Like the holiday season. According to a recent study by Payless Power , running a full display throughout December costs $15.36 with LED lights and $92.03 with incandescent lights at the typical electricity rate. That’s a $76.67 difference. Where you live can affect your electric bill, too. Hawaii is the most expensive state for holiday lighting, at $42.53 for a full LED display and $254.84 for the incandescent version. Rhode Island ($31.85), Massachusetts ($31.47), Maine ($30.98), and New Hampshire ($26.81) also make the list of the five most expensive states for a full LED display. Meanwhile, homeowners in North Dakota ($11.25), Nebraska ($11.49), and Missouri ($12.02) pay the least. The good news is there are ways to lower your electric bill without sacrificing curb appeal or holiday spirit, regardless of where you live. All it takes is a bit of planning and creativity. Loading... Payless Power priced 13 common lights and decorations individually, each running for six hours per night for 31 nights at the typical U.S. rate of 15 cents per kilowatt-hour. Payless Power What’s causing the hikes? A variety of factors are contributing to high electric bills these days. “The grid is outdated. Infrastructure is old, and utility companies need to replace and upgrade equipment,” says Brandon Young , CEO of Payless Power in Fort Worth, TX . Extreme weather plays a huge role as well, as the lines and equipment can’t always handle conditions like freezing temperatures and high winds. Increased electricity demand adds to the problem. “Demand is growing, and the grid can’t always keep up. Data centers and industrial use are large consumers of energy, and it takes a lot to power those facilities,” Young explains. Fuel costs also fluctuate and affect how much it costs to generate electricity. “Prices for residential customers in 2025 went up more than twice the rate of inflation,” says Young. These high costs are particularly noticeable during the holiday season. Young points out that many homeowners often forget that a higher utility rate doesn’t take December off. “The higher rate is there all year, and every kilowatt-hour is more costly. The oven and lights for holiday gatherings all cost more to use,” Young adds. How to trim your electric bill without skimping on holiday fun Fortunately, you don’t have to forgo Christmas lights altogether. These tips can help you enjoy them while keeping your electricity costs in check. Use LED lights While you don’t get to choose your utility rates, you do get to choose your light bulbs. And LEDs are much cheaper than incandescent bulbs. “One hundred bulb C9s cost about $19.57 in December to run, and if they're swapped with LEDs, you’ll pay $2.80,” says Young. LED lights aren’t hard to find either. You'll notice a variety of options at just about any home improvement store. Give your lights a break You don’t have to keep your lights on all day, every day. Consider displaying them only from 5 to 10 p.m., for example. You could use a timer or smart plug that allows you to turn them on or off manually when you want to. Also, if you plan to leave town, keep them off until you return. Don’t go overboard Lighting every bush in your yard will cost you. Instead, be selective about where you hang lights. Highlighting your front door, roof line, and a tree in your yard can make just as big of an impact. Unplug your inflatables (or use light projectors instead) If you have inflatables, there’s no reason to keep them on 24/7. “Unplugging inflatables when you go to bed saves a few dollars. The cost to leave one up for the month is about $1.68, which is a lot to pay [compared with] a 100-bulb LED light strand at 14 cents,” says Young. In addition, you don’t have to use inflatables for your home to stand out. A light projector can do the trick at a fraction of the cost. The study says that a projector costs only 17 cents per month to run, compared to $1.68 for an inflatable.

items.title: BNPL for rent seeks a market
items.description: BNPL for rent seeks a market A new crop of fintechs is exploring growth opportunities in pay-later lending for monthly rent payments as inflation pinches consumers. Published Nov. 11, 2026 Justin Bachman Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Apartment buildings in Lower Manhattan, New York. Several fintech startups are drawing renters with pay-later services to cover monthly rent payments. Getty Images First published on Listen to the article 13 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Pay-later loans are increasingly available for monthly housing payments as financial technology companies seek growth by responding to consumers’ affordability struggles. While the buy now, pay later market has traditionally focused on providing consumers with financing at retail merchants for discretionary items, a newer batch of companies sees profit potential in tailoring loans to rental payments and other monthly bills such as utilities, medical care and telephone service. A variety of players have moved into the pay-later rental arena in recent years, aiming to fill financial gaps between consumers’ monthly rents and their incomes, as the increases in the former outpace the latter. Ariel Nelson Permission granted by National Consumer Law Center The rise of these businesses is “really revealing in what they say about the state of affordability around life essentials,” said Ariel Nelson, a senior attorney with the National Consumer Law Center. “These products are really appealing because people are desperate.” Companies seeking to develop a market in the rental area include RealPage, an apartment management software firm, which last year bought Livble , a startup that offers renters flexible payment options. Another is New York-based Flexible Finance, known as Flex, which lets consumers split their rent, mortgage or other monthly bill payments. A third rent-focused fintech is Bilt Technologies, which offers a payments and loyalty program aimed at attracting rent and mortgage payments to credit cards, including its co-branded cards. In addition to points for rent and everyday spending on cards, New York-based Bilt issues points for homeowners’ association and condominium fee payments. Bilt members can transfer the points to 18 airline and seven hotel loyalty partner programs to redeem for flights and hotel stays. The points can also be redeemed at merchants such as Amazon.com and Lyft. Consumer advocates contend that pay-later products aimed at rent and medical care can exacerbate financial strains for economically vulnerable people and lead to a stacking of their debt. “As the price of shelter has shot up, a new breed of predatory creditors has emerged aiming to turn this emergency into profit,” advocacy group Protect Borrowers said in a February report on the rent now, pay later industry . “Beneath the surface, these products are united in being little more than a repackaging of an age-old debt trap: payday loans.” About 109 million Americans have a monthly rental payment, according to Protect Borrowers, a Washington-based nonprofit that lobbies and litigates on consumer debt issues. The group was formed in 2018 as the Student Borrower Protection Center by former officials of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Pay-later options allow renters to avoid being late on their rent, avoiding landlords’ late fees and revolving credit card interest rates that can reach 30% or more, Zahir Khoja, RealPage’s chief fintech officer, said in an interview last month. The average late fee is $85, he said. “It’s not that you can’t pay your rent,” he said of tenant customers that select pay-later plans. “You may not be able to pay your rent on January 1st, and so you need some time in the month of January to be able to do it. It’s much better than paying a late fee or revolving at 29.9 (percent) on credit.” Another BNPL provider, Sydney-based Zip, offers a bill-payment service to split monthly bills such as insurance, utilities and mobile phone. The company is also exploring a new rent-focused service for the U.S. market. Many “everyday Americans” are challenged by a misalignment between the timing of their income and bills, Zip’s former U.S. CEO, Joe Heck, told analysts on the BNPL provider’s August earnings call. Heck left Zip last month, the company said in an Oct. 16 investor announcement . “Most consumers are paid every two weeks, while bills like rent are generally due monthly,” Heck said. “That mismatch in timing of income and expenses creates large opportunities beyond BNPL,” he said, pointing to bill payments and the need for “income-smoothing” as other ways the services could be used. The company offers both Livble and Flex via its app for residents and property managers or owners. items.title: OCTOBER CHILL BRINGS COOLER SALES, MORE CHOICES FOR HOUSTON BUYERS
items.description: OCTOBER CHILL BRINGS COOLER SALES, MORE CHOICES FOR HOUSTON BUYERS Home prices hold steady as supply reaches a 14-year high HOUSTON -- (November 11, 2026) -- The Greater Houston housing market saw a change in pace in October, offering buyers more choices while sellers adjusted to a shift in activity. According to the Houston Association of Realtors' October 2026 Housing Market Update, single-family home sales were 14.9% below last year's level, with 6,348 homes sold. The average home price held steady in October at $421,100, while the median price declined 3.0% to $320,000, its lowest level since January 2024. The number of homes on the market remained near record levels, with 40,253 single-family homes for sale, up 6.8% from last October. "Consumers are paying close attention to the economy and their household budgets, so it is understandable that some buyers are taking more time before purchasing a home," said HAR Chair Theresa Hill with Compass RE Texas, LLC - Houston. "We typically see activity ease as the year winds down, but buyers who are still looking may have more time to find a home that fits their needs and budget." Housing Market Overview Across all property types, 7,485 properties were sold in October, down 15.1% compared with a year earlier. Total dollar volume dipped 14.6% to $3.06 billion. The number of active listings across all property types increased 4.8% to 61,965 Despite October's decline, single-family home sales through the first 10 months of 2026 remained within 2% of last year's pace. Stronger sales during the spring and early summer helped offset the declines recorded in recent months. Single-Family Homes Update In October, 6,348 single-family homes sold across the Houston area, compared with 7,458 during the same time last year. That represents a decline of 14.9%. October's single-family home sales were the fewest for any October in the past 10 years. However, total sales over the prior 12 months reached 87,433, remaining above the 2019 level of 85,685, the last normal year before the pandemic. The average price was virtually unchanged at $421,100. The median price was $320,000, which is 3.0% below last year's level. It is the lowest median price for any October since 2021, with an October peak of $335,000 in 2024. The average mortgage rate in October was 7.33%, up 108 basis points from a year ago, but still below the 7.62% recorded in October 2023. Buyers of a median-priced home paid an estimated monthly mortgage payment (including principal and interest) of $1,760.28. That is $134.79 more than a year ago but less than the $1,845.03 paid in October 2023, when both rates and median home prices were higher. "Affordability remains a challenge for homebuyers, and the possibility of a quarter-point interest rate increase by the Federal Reserve before the end of the year could add further pressure to the housing market," said HAR Chief Economist Ted C. Jones. Homes spent an average of 59 days on the market, unchanged from last October. Pending sales, which represent homes under contract but not yet sold, declined 17.6% to 6,445. The market had a 5.5-month supply of single-family homes, unchanged from September and its highest level since 2012. Nationwide, there was a 4.8 months' supply, according to the National Association of Realtors. Broken out by housing segments, single-family home sales performed as follows: $1 - $99,999: increased 2.1% (97 transactions) $100,000 - $149,999: decreased 1.0% (191 transactions) $150,000 - $249,999: decreased 9.4% (1,339 transactions) $250,000 - $499,999: decreased 16.8% (3,368 transactions) $500,000 - $999,999: decreased 16.9% (1,061 transactions) $1M and above: decreased 11.6% (291 transactions) HAR also reports on existing single-family home sales, which fell 10.2% in October. The average price declined slightly to $428,790, while the median price was down 4.5% to $315,000. HAR will publish its October 2026 Rental Market Update on Wednesday, November 18. For HAR's Monthly Activity Snapshot of the October 2026 trends, please CLICK HERE to access a downloadable PDF file. Townhome/Condominium Update The townhome and condominium market also recorded fewer sales in October. Sales declined 23.5% year over year, with 336 properties sold compared with 439 last October. The average sales price increased 5.8% to $263,413, while the median price declined 3.7% to $197,500. Active listings climbed 5.6% to 3,586 properties. The supply of townhomes and condominiums expanded from 8.2 months to 9.4 months, while days on market edged up to 65 days. Houston Real Estate Highlights in October Single-family home sales declined 14.9% year over year. Pending single-family sales declined 17.6% to 6,445. Active single-family listings increased 6.8% to 40,253. The average single-family home price was flat at $421,100. The median single-family home price declined 3.0% to $320,000, its lowest level since January 2024. Single-family homes took an average of 59 days to sell, unchanged from last year. The supply of single-family homes increased from 5.1 months to 5.5 months. Total property sales declined 15.1%, with 7,485 transactions. Total dollar volume declined 14.6% to $3.06 billion. items.title: October 2026 Central Texas Housing Report
items.description: October 2026 Central Texas Housing Report 11/11/2026 Central Texas home sales decline in October as buyers navigate affordability challenges AUSTIN, Texas — According to the October 2026 Central Texas Housing Report released by Unlock MLS , closed sales across the Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos MSA declined 11.4% year over year to 2,114. The median home sales price declined 6.9% to $404,802 following months of relatively stable pricing, which can be attributed to lower-priced homes accounting for a greater share of sales. Demand remained strongest among homes priced between $200,000 and $299,000, underscoring how affordability continues to shape buyer activity. Vaike O'Grady, market research advisor at Unlock MLS, said affordability challenges continue to weigh on the Central Texas housing market, even as resale homes become more competitive with new construction. “Despite another softer month, year-to-date home sales are up 2.5% compared with the same period last year, and while overall pending sales declined 4.0% year over year, pending resale contracts increased 6%. Builders have relied on incentives such as price reductions and mortgage rate buydowns to attract buyers, but that competitive advantage may be narrowing. This shift suggests resale activity is gaining traction as buyers continue to weigh affordability and value in their homebuying decisions.” John Crowe , 2026 Unlock MLS and ABoR president, emphasized that softer home prices and slower sales may give buyers greater negotiating flexibility, while sellers must remain competitive with their pricing and expectations. “The data is an important starting point, but understanding the factors behind the numbers is what helps buyers and sellers determine when the time is right for them. A professional agent can help buyers and sellers understand what's driving market trends, how conditions differ by county and what this all means for making their next move.
